name: Economic Security Project (charityevals' estimate)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: lower-income US families, through state tax credits, guaranteed income pilots and public options.
summary: Economic Security Project's 501(c)(3), a US non-profit spending about $10 million a year, campaigns for state child and earned income tax credits, guaranteed income, the IRS's free Direct File service and public options such as city-run grocery stores. Its average year of spending over 2022-2024 is counted against a share of the $3.6 billion a year of state tax credits enacted in those years (15% caused by advocates, 13% of the advocates' resources its own), valued for lower-income families net of what the credits cost state taxpayers; guaranteed income pilots, Direct File (whose $73 million cost to taxpayers outweighs what it gave its users) and a planned public grocery store in Chicago add little. With its next dollar at {{row:marginal_vs_past_average}} of the average, it comes to about {{result}} years of healthy life per 1,000 dollars. The result is mostly uncertainty: how much of the credits the advocates caused and Economic Security Project's share of them are judgments from the research on advocacy, and every branch is discounted by the shared missing-data slider.

sections.title: Cost
sections.explainer: What the modelled program cost in the year the outcomes below are counted for, including its share of overhead. From audited financial statements or the annual report.

sections.title: Reach
sections.explainer: How many people, animals or meals the spending reached in the same year, as the charity reports it.

sections.title: Effect per unit
sections.explainer: What the intervention does for each unit reached, from the best available studies, before any adjustment.

sections.title: Adjustments
sections.explainer: Discounts for weaker evidence, what would have happened anyway, credit shared with others, and delivery falling short. All multiply the outcome.

sections.title: Value of a dollar moved (shared)
sections.explainer: charityevals' shared method for money a meta charity moves, the same rows in every such model (docs/normalization.md 2.8). A dollar moved is worth what the charities it reaches achieve, each at its live result on this site under your values; new money counts in full, shifted money only for the gain over where it would have gone.

sections.title: Career changes
sections.explainer: People the charity moves into high-impact jobs: per career changed, the pay they give up for the years they stay, valued at the new employer's live result per dollar, times the share of changes the charity caused (docs/normalization.md 2.8). The mirror of staff pay below market.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.explainer: The outcome in the family's shared unit, per dollar.

sections.title: Your dollar's share
sections.explainer: Staff who earn less than they could elsewhere pay part of the cost in kind. With credit by share of resources, your dollar is credited with its share of the full cost only.

source.quote: These filers claimed more than $90 million in refunds and saved an estimated $5.6 million in tax preparation fees

rows.explainer: All refunds filed through the pilot; most were owed anyway and would have been claimed through another route.

rows.label: IRS Direct File: share of its refunds claimed only because of it (credits from people who wouldn't otherwise have filed)
rows.explainer: Treasury's user survey found 16% of users hadn't filed the year before (the same page), the high end, since most of them would have filed some other way; the IRS puts Earned Income Tax Credit take-up near 78%, and most free filers would have claimed anyway: 0.07, the best guess, our judgment. Range 0.02 to 0.16.

rows.label: IRS Direct File: credits newly claimed, both seasons (US$)
rows.explainer: The 2024 refund per return applied to both seasons, times the share newly claimed: about $20 million, a transfer from federal taxpayers.

rows.label: IRS Direct File: users' savings and new credits less the programme's and credits' cost to taxpayers, ln(consumption)
rows.explainer: A dollar saved, received or paid is worth one over the consumption of who saves, receives or pays it (the small-change form of the log scale): about $18 million saved and $20 million of credits newly claimed by moderate-income users, against $73 million of programme cost and the credits' cost to federal taxpayers. Slightly negative: the service cost taxpayers more dollars than it gave its users, more than its users being poorer than those who pay makes up for. Users' time saved and tax-preparation firms' lost margins (borne by richer shareholders) are left out and roughly offset.

rows.label: IRS Direct File: net value of its two seasons, per year of work (units of value)
rows.explainer: Counted for the two seasons it ran, not the years a won reform counts: it was suspended in October 2025, so its years in force are its whole result. Spread over the three years of work.

rows.label: IRS Direct File: users' gross savings and new credits, per year of work (units of value)
Guaranteed income pilots: recipients' consumption per person (US$ a year)
rows.explainer: The site's survey-consumption base for US households near or below the poverty line (the shared share for food-aid recipients, 30%, range 20-50%): the pilots' recipients reported household incomes of $19,242 on average (Corinth and Mayhew, Table 2), about $6,400 a person, which understates what poor households consume.

rows.label: Guaranteed income pilots: yearly payment per person in a recipient household (US$)
Guaranteed income pilots: ln(consumption) gain per person per year of payments
rows.explainer: About {{row:gi_gross_ln_per_person_year}}. The large-pilot employment fall (-3 points, the paper's Table 3) takes a little of the gain, in gi_evidence_adj.

rows.label: Guaranteed income pilots: value of what the money would otherwise have funded, as a share of its value as cash
rows.explainer: The pilots were paid from cities' American Rescue Plan funds and from philanthropy, both of which would have been spent on something else: payers' cost is the same either way, so the gain is the cash's value less the alternative's. Spent on average residents, a dollar is worth about a tenth of one to these households (their survey consumption per person, about $9,800, against national consumption of $58,517); spent on other services for low-income residents, close to the same. 0.4, range 0.1 to 0.9.

rows.explainer: A flow: each year's pilot payments count once, against a year of spending (Convention 3).

Public grocery stores: ln(consumption) gain per resident per year, net of the city's subsidy
rows.explainer: A new full-service store in a food desert lowers shopping time and prices a little but barely changes what people eat (Allcott, Diamond and Dubé 2019, Quarterly Journal of Economics: entry closes about a tenth of the healthy-eating gap); a city-run store also needs a subsidy that falls on taxpayers. 0.003 a year (about $40 per person at these residents' consumption), range -0.002 (subsidy above the savings) to 0.012.

rows.label: Public grocery stores: chance Chicago opens its planned store
rows.explainer: The shared chance a lobbied issue changes (@democracy.lobbied_issue_change_rate, 0.4) moved by the record: Chicago's mayor proposed the store in 2023 and the feasibility study was done in 2024, but no site or budget had been settled by 2026. 0.3, range 0.1 to 0.5.

rows.label: Public grocery stores: years until a store opens
rows.explainer: No study measures how long public grocery stores take to open, so there is no reference class. Siting, financing and building a store: three years, from one (taking over an existing store) to five.

State tax credits: share that wouldn't have come at all, or not for years, without the advocates
rows.explainer: The research on whether advocacy changes policy: Baumgartner, Berry, Hojnacki, Kimball and Leech (2009, Lobbying and Policy Change, 98 random US federal issues) find about 60% of campaigns change nothing and resources explain under 5% of who wins. The credits of 2022-2024 came as the expanded federal credit lapsed and states had record surpluses; governors and legislators who wanted them carried most, and the state campaigns for them shaped their size and refundability. 0.15, range 0.05 to 0.35.

rows.label: State tax credits: Economic Security Project's (501(c)(3)) share of the advocates' resources behind the credits
rows.explainer: The state campaigns were run by state fiscal policy institutes and anti-poverty coalitions (the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities' State Priorities Partnership of 40-odd state groups, the Institute on Taxation and Economic Policy, children's advocates), with Economic Security Project as funder, strategist and national coordinator ($0.69 million of its 2024 grants went through the campaigns line, plus staff, polling and messaging). Its sister 501(c)(4), Economic Security Project Action, lobbied for the same credits (about $1.8 million of its $3.6 million in 2024 on its campaigns line) and counts among the other advocates here, since only the 501(c)(3) is modelled. The 501(c)(3)'s campaign spending (about $2.5 million a year plus affiliate work) against the 501(c)(4)'s and tens of millions a year across the state groups: 0.13, range 0.04 to 0.27.

rows.label: State tax credits: share of credit used
rows.explainer: The share among co-advocates times the mobiliser's share: the rest of the credit stays with those who carry out the result (docs/normalization.md 2.24).

rows.label: State tax credits: how much of the counted money is real
rows.explainer: The yearly figures are Economic Security Project's own sums of states' fiscal notes, not independently tallied, and a few improvements may be one-off rebates counted as yearly money. Whether the credits last is in the shared years a won reform counts, not here. 0.8, range 0.6 to 0.95.

rows.label: IRS Direct File: share that wouldn't have happened without the advocates
rows.explainer: The research on whether advocacy changes policy: Baumgartner, Berry, Hojnacki, Kimball and Leech (2009, Lobbying and Policy Change, 98 random US federal issues) find about 60% of campaigns change nothing and resources explain under 5% of who wins. The Inflation Reduction Act of 2022 funded the IRS's study and Treasury chose to build it; a coalition of advocates (Code for America, the Center for American Progress, Economic Security Project and others) pressed for it for years against the tax-preparation industry. 0.3, range 0.1 to 0.6.

rows.label: IRS Direct File: Economic Security Project's share of the advocates' resources
rows.explainer: One of several national groups; Code for America built tools for it. 0.1, range 0.03 to 0.25.

rows.label: IRS Direct File: share of credit used
rows.explainer: The share among co-advocates times the mobiliser's share: the rest of the credit stays with those who carry out the result (docs/normalization.md 2.24).

rows.label: Guaranteed income pilots: share that wouldn't have happened without the guaranteed income movement
rows.explainer: Cities chose to spend pandemic money on cash pilots because the movement (Stockton's pilot, which Economic Security Project funded, then Mayors for a Guaranteed Income) had made the case; some would have tried cash anyway after the federal stimulus. 0.5, range 0.2 to 0.8.

rows.label: Guaranteed income pilots: Economic Security Project's share of the movement's resources
rows.explainer: Among those who organise and argue for the pilots: in 2022-2024 Mayors for a Guaranteed Income and local organisers (with GiveDirectly and others delivering) ran most of the pilots, and the OpenResearch study was independent; no count of the organisers' budgets was found; Economic Security Project, which seeded the first pilots, now convenes the national coalition, runs the Guaranteed Income Now conference and research, with about $1.8 million a year. The cities and funders whose money pays the transfers (philanthropic gifts such as Jack Dorsey's $18 million in 2020 among them) are the adopters: their part is under the mobiliser's share, not in this one (docs/normalization.md 2.24). 0.15, range 0.05 to 0.35.

rows.label: Guaranteed income pilots: share of credit used
rows.explainer: The share among co-advocates times the mobiliser's share: the rest of the credit stays with those who carry out the result (docs/normalization.md 2.24).

rows.label: Guaranteed income pilots: how much of the modelled gain is real
rows.explainer: The large pilots cut employment about 3 points (income elasticity -0.18, Corinth and Mayhew Table 3), a little of the gain taken back in leisure that is worth something itself. 0.9, range 0.6 to 1.

rows.label: Public grocery stores: share of a store that wouldn't open without the public-option advocates
rows.explainer: Chicago's mayor and Venice's council drive the plans; the feasibility study and campaign made a public store an option they could fund through the state's grocery grants. 0.5, range 0.2 to 0.8.

rows.label: Public grocery stores: Economic Security Project's share of the advocates' resources
rows.explainer: It commissioned the feasibility study with HR&A for the city and campaigned for public grocery stores in Illinois; its Illinois affiliate (outside these accounts) and local activists urged the city and state to fund stores. The mayor's office, which would open the store, is the adopter: its part is under the mobiliser's share, not in this one (docs/normalization.md 2.24). 0.5, range 0.2 to 0.8.

rows.label: Public grocery stores: share of credit used
rows.explainer: The share among co-advocates times the mobiliser's share: the rest of the credit stays with those who carry out the result (docs/normalization.md 2.24).

rows.label: Public grocery stores: how much of the modelled reach and gain is real
rows.explainer: The people served is an order-of-magnitude judgment and the store's design is unsettled. 0.7, range 0.3 to 1.

rows.label: State tax credits: discount for missing data
rows.explainer: Thin: no measured outcome for Economic Security Project's part; the money and reach are counts, but the share caused is a judgment from the research on advocacy.

Side effect: children's long-run gains from family income, as a share of the families' gross value
rows.explainer: Income in childhood raises children's later earnings and health beyond the year's consumption (Hoynes, Schanzenbach and Almond 2016; the National Academies' 2019 Roadmap to Reducing Child Poverty). 0.1, range 0 to 0.3: these are cash credits for families with children.

rows.label: Side effect: work effects of the credits, as a share of the families' gross value
rows.explainer: Earned income credits draw people into work (Eissa and Liebman 1996); child credits without a work requirement reduce it a little. Mixed: 0.01, range -0.05 to 0.05.

rows.label: Side effect: the pilots' evidence and lasting programmes, as a share of the pilots' gross value
rows.explainer: Pilots turned into lasting programmes (Cook County's, made permanent in 2024; California's state-funded pilots) and the evidence feeds the case for wider cash policy, which the model doesn't value directly. 0.3, range 0 to 1.5, our judgment.
